title: An interface that makes inaccessible software operable through a user’s chosen modality

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a general interface layer that lets people understand and operate existing software through input and output modalities suited to them, including software that has not been adapted for their access needs. It would communicate task-relevant information, expose available actions, carry out the user’s choices, and support correction while preserving meaning. Its defining capability would be faithful, controllable access across applications, rather than a separate adaptation built for each application. This describes a research goal, not an achieved system.

The interface would need to preserve the user’s understanding of what is happening: which application and control are active, what has changed, what an action will do, and how to recover from an error. The supplied A11y-CUA review documents difficulties involving focus, context, multi-application workflows, recovery, and accessible agent feedback. These findings motivate a layer that maintains shared context and lets users invite assistance without surrendering their established workflows.

A broader proposed requirement is handling interfaces with inadequate semantic information. Charts, custom controls, and changing layouts are candidate challenges: the layer would have to determine what matters to the task and communicate it without silently altering its meaning. The supplied study does not establish how widespread these semantic deficiencies are or demonstrate their general solution. Where the necessary information is unavailable, the interface would need to disclose that limitation instead of inventing an interpretation.

significance.text: If achieved across previously unadapted software, this capability would substantially expand independent access to computing. Users could pursue consequential workflows through modalities that work for them, with less dependence on application-specific adaptations or another person’s intervention. The revolutionary contribution would be the combination of broad software coverage, faithful communication, and user-directed operation. This is a conditional assessment of the proposed capability, not a population-scale impact demonstrated by the supplied study.

Choice and control are essential to that benefit. The reviewed study describes preferences for assistance that augments existing workflows, can be invited when useful, explains its actions accessibly, and supports easy undo. An interface that completes tasks while leaving users unable to follow, redirect, or correct its behavior would fall short of the proposed innovation’s purpose.

As a downstream possibility, reliable deployment could broaden participation in work, education, and services that depend on software. Such effects would also depend on privacy, affordability, deployment constraints, and coverage of real applications. The layer would complement accessible software design: better native semantics and controls would still improve the information available to it. An analogy to a universal translator has limits because interface access involves action, changing state, and consequences, and no translation layer can reconstruct information that is inherently unavailable.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability proposed here is dependable translation between an application’s task-relevant state and a user’s chosen interaction modality, coupled with reliable operation and correction. This requires more than recognizing visible controls: the system must preserve relationships, available choices, consequences, and changes over time. The supplied evidence does not establish whether any existing system already delivers this complete capability across a defined scope, so its present-day absence cannot be asserted from this record alone.

The reviewed study identifies concrete barriers relevant to that goal. Switching applications could reset focus and navigation landmarks, forcing blind and low-vision users to rebuild context. Limited accessible feedback and difficulties with recovery also complicate collaboration with computer use agents. A successful layer would therefore need to keep the user’s context aligned with application state, communicate progress and errors, and support a recoverable handoff between user and agent.

Engineering synthesis: broader coverage would require distinguishing information actually exposed by the application from information inferred from appearance, then communicating uncertainty at the point where it matters. Charts and custom controls may require task-specific interpretation; dynamic interfaces require tracking changes without losing context; personalized presentation requires changing how information is conveyed without changing its substance. Supporting varied sensory and motor needs adds distinct input, output, timing, and correction requirements. These are proposed barriers for the broader concept, not capabilities tested comprehensively by the supplied study.

current_state.text: Screen readers and other assistive technologies already enable extensive computer use. The supplied 2026 study, “A11y-CUA Dataset: Characterizing the Accessibility Gap in Computer Use Agents,” by Ananya Gubbi Mohanbabu, Rosiana Natalie, Brandon Kim, Anhong Guo, and Amy Pavel, is identified as a CHI 2026 paper with DOI 10.1145/3772318.3791896. It examines blind and low-vision users and computer use agents in controlled Windows tasks. Every benchmark task was validated as feasible through both mouse-driven and keyboard-centric workflows, so the study does not demonstrate access to software that was otherwise inoperable with existing assistive interaction.

Across 60 tasks, both tested models had lower aggregate task success under keyboard-only and magnified-viewport conditions than under their default configurations. The supplied review reports Claude Sonnet 4.5 success of 78.33%, 41.67%, and 28.33%, respectively, and Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct success of 20%, 0%, and 0%. Table 4 presents the Sonnet values at lower precision as 78.3%, 41.6%, and 28.3%. Taken together, the reviewed abstract, methods, Table 4, and Sections 5.1–5.2 support the aggregate ordering; the small reporting differences should not be read as independently measured outcomes.

The experimental constraints matter. In the condition labelled for screen-reader use, NVDA was running and the agent retained full-desktop screenshots and keyboard actions, but it could not use screen-reader feedback or access the accessibility tree. The results therefore cannot be described as a test of an agent perceiving the interface through a screen reader. They show performance under particular assistive-interaction constraints and an accessibility gap in the tested agents, rather than testing the general interface layer proposed here. Extension to other operating systems, otherwise inaccessible software, missing semantics, and varied motor access needs remains untested in this evidence.

The evidence available through the supplied review is partial: its text extraction ends mid-table on page 22 of a stated 26-page document, and Figure 8 was unavailable for inspection. The performance comparison above relies on the reviewed textual results and Table 4. The review also identifies internal inconsistencies in category-level magnifier reporting, which limit detailed category interpretation without reversing the reported aggregate ordering. No supplied freshness search establishes coverage through November 1, 2026; the paper’s dated results remain informative, but this record cannot establish the latest state of the field.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: participants with varied sensory and motor access needs would complete consequential workflows in independently selected, previously unseen applications and documents using their preferred input and output. The evaluation should include software requiring adaptation by the layer and use meaningful accessible native alternatives as comparators where available. Outcomes would include task success, time, error recovery, privacy, and autonomy. The tested applications, modalities, operating environments, and assistance allowed should define the demonstrated scope; finite testing would establish breadth within that scope, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Users complete unseen application workflows using their preferred modalities

completion_criteria.text: The supplied study recommends reporting assistive-technology configuration, task success, action counts, elapsed time, and perception, cognitive, and action errors for each task and condition. Those measurements provide a useful foundation for evaluating whether an interface layer improves usable access and where its failures arise. They should be interpreted alongside the user’s ability to understand the system’s state and recover control, rather than treating completion alone as sufficient.
completion_criteria.label: Report task-level access measurements alongside state understanding and control

completion_criteria.text: Proposed fidelity and control tests should check whether the interface preserves task-relevant meaning, communicates consequential state changes, and lets users inspect, redirect, correct, and undo actions where the underlying application permits. Cases with missing information should test whether the system identifies what it cannot recover and communicates the practical consequence. A successful evaluation should distinguish faithful interpretation from a plausible guess that happens to produce the expected task outcome.
completion_criteria.label: Preserve task-relevant meaning with user control and disclosed information gaps

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements include independently repeated evaluations with documented application versions, configurations, task selection, and failure cases, followed by testing across additional applications and users. A later protocol should set acceptance thresholds for reliability, recovery, and practical overhead before testing, with justification appropriate to the consequences of each workflow. No numerical completion threshold is established by the supplied evidence. Practical boundaries should state when the layer needs native accessibility support, additional user input, or access it does not possess, and what privacy conditions are required.
completion_criteria.label: Independently reproduce evaluations with documented conditions and practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: HCI-01, “A predictive science of human–computer interaction,” could supply methods for anticipating performance and evaluating modality choices, while HCI-04 concerns delivering operational access. HCI-02, “Reliable communication and computer control after profound paralysis,” overlaps in enabling computer operation under severe motor constraints; it centers on obtaining reliable communication and control signals, whereas HCI-04 centers on making application content and actions usable through the chosen channel.

Roster-based synthesis: HCI-03, “A general-purpose, high-fidelity interface for touch and physical force,” could provide an input or output modality for HCI-04, but developing physical feedback is a separate breakthrough from interpreting software. HCI-07, “Everyday visual computing with perceptually convincing spatial displays,” concerns visual display capabilities; HCI-04 must support access choices across modalities and does not depend on spatial displays.

Roster-based synthesis: HCI-05, “End-user programming that ordinary users can understand and maintain,” overlaps in letting users adapt computing to their needs, but concerns understandable, maintainable programs rather than access to existing interfaces. HCI-06, “Delegation interfaces that keep people in meaningful control of computer work,” shares requirements for understandable agent actions, correction, and user control. HCI-04 additionally requires faithful access through a user’s chosen modality, including workflows the user operates directly.

Roster-based synthesis: HCI-08, “Real-time conversational interfaces across signed and spoken languages,” overlaps in modality and language access, but translating human conversation is distinct from interpreting software state and executing application actions. HCI-09, “Privacy controls that remain understandable and enforceable across services,” addresses protections that could be important when an interface layer observes or operates sensitive workflows; those controls are a separate capability from making software operable.

Roster-based synthesis: HCI-10, “Lifelong personal memory augmentation with controllable evidence,” could support retained preferences and context, but maintaining a durable personal memory differs from interpreting current application state faithfully. HCI-11, “Remote collaboration with usable shared social and spatial cues,” overlaps in maintaining shared understanding and communicating changes; its focus is collaboration between people, whereas HCI-04 focuses on access between a person and software. These relationships preserve each roster entry as a distinct innovation.

change_log.change: Preserved HCI-04’s ID, title, and general interface-layer identity while explicitly describing it as a proposed capability.
change_log.reason: The supplied study motivates parts of the concept but does not demonstrate the complete innovation or establish its present-day absence.

change_log.change: Replaced the broad prevalence claim about missing software semantics with documented focus, context, feedback, and recovery barriers; retained semantic interpretation as a broader research requirement.
change_log.reason: The review supports specific interaction problems but does not establish how often software lacks reliable semantics or test general transformation of charts and custom controls.

change_log.change: Corrected the description of the screen-reader-labelled experiment to keyboard-only interaction with screenshots, NVDA running, and no access to screen-reader feedback or the accessibility tree.
change_log.reason: Calling it screen-reader-mediated perception would misrepresent the experimental condition.

change_log.change: Added model-specific results across all three conditions, the 60-task scope, and the reported precision differences.
change_log.reason: The reviewed evidence supports the aggregate comparison and provides quantitative detail that should be preserved without concealing reporting differences.

change_log.change: Replaced reliance on Figure 8 with the reviewed abstract, methods, Table 4, and textual results, and preserved extraction and category-reporting limitations.
change_log.reason: Figure 8 was unavailable in the partial extraction; other reviewed passages support the aggregate finding.

change_log.change: Clarified that benchmark tasks were already feasible with existing assistive interaction and limited the demonstrated scope to the studied Windows setting.
change_log.reason: The study does not establish access to otherwise inoperable software or generalization across operating systems and access needs.

change_log.change: Expanded completion criteria to include meaning preservation, declared uncertainty, reproducibility, justified acceptance thresholds, and practical boundaries.
change_log.reason: These integrate the review’s recommendations while keeping new evaluation requirements explicitly proposed.

change_log.change: Separated direct conditional benefits from downstream adoption possibilities and explained relationships to every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: This preserves the concept’s significance and identity without overstating demonstrated impact or merging distinct innovations.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish the prevalence of inadequate software semantics or whether the full proposed capability remains unavailable across a defined scope.
Generalization to otherwise inaccessible software, other operating systems, and varied sensory and motor access needs remains untested in the supplied record.

The extraction is truncated, Figure 8 was unavailable, and category-level magnifier inconsistencies remain unresolved. Minor differences in reported aggregate precision also remain in the supplied review.
No supplied freshness search establishes field coverage through November 1, 2026, or supports a claim that the cited study represents the latest work.

A decisive evaluation still needs specified application coverage, participant representation, meaningful native comparators, and justified acceptance thresholds; these are not established standards in the supplied evidence.

brief.title: Software access in the way that works for you
possible: You could operate software that does not support your access needs, using your preferred way of giving instructions and receiving information. A shared interface would explain available actions, carry out your choices, and help you correct mistakes across applications.

You could follow what changed, understand what an action would do, and take back control when needed. Changing how software communicates with you would preserve the meaning of its information and choices.
why: People with sensory or motor access needs could complete more computing tasks independently, with less reliance on another person or a separate adaptation for each application.

Broader access could expand participation in work, education, and services that depend on software. Keeping users informed and in control would let assistance support their decisions and established ways of working.

sources.who: University of California, Berkeley and University of Michigan
sources.showed: The researchers compared human computer use with AI agents that operate software. Agents completed fewer tasks when restricted to keyboard input or a magnified view.
sources.quote:
The default CUA exe-
cuted 78.3% of tasks successfully.
sources.cited_for: Current agents struggle under interaction constraints relevant to blind and low-vision users.
sources.not_established: The tasks were already operable through existing access methods, and agents did not receive screen-reader feedback.

sources.who: Stony Brook University and Old Dominion University
sources.showed: In a small preprint study, blind users tried OLLA, an accessible interface to software-operating agents. The best model completed 52.5% of commands successfully.
sources.quote:
Trace analysis reveals
grounding, planning, constraint-tracking, and
termination failures, while interviews reveal
beyond-automation needs.
sources.cited_for: Accessible agent interfaces can support everyday desktop use, but execution remains unreliable.
sources.not_established: The study does not establish reliable access for people with other sensory or motor needs.

sources.who: Stony Brook University and Old Dominion University
sources.showed: Savant translated everyday language into sequences of screen-reader actions. A small study with blind participants found faster access to application controls.
sources.quote: Participants were also able to access application controls nearly 4 times faster on average than with screen readers alone while doing these tasks.
sources.cited_for: A consistent command interface can reduce the effort of navigating different applications.
sources.not_established: Faster control access does not establish faithful, recoverable operation across previously unadapted software.

sources.showed: Screen Recognition inferred descriptions of controls from screen images for VoiceOver, a screen reader that presents interface content without sight. Participants could use some previously inaccessible mobile apps.
sources.quote:
In a study with 9 screen reader
users, we validated that our approach improves the accessibility of
existing mobile apps, enabling even previously inaccessible apps to
be used.
sources.cited_for: Interpreting screen images can restore some access when applications omit descriptions needed by accessibility tools.
sources.not_established: Visible content cannot reveal every available action, including gestures with no visible cue.

sources.who: Carnegie Mellon University, Adobe Research and UC Berkeley
sources.showed: Morae paused software automation when users needed to make choices. A small study found better task completion and choices that better matched users’ preferences.
sources.quote:
Users reported a stronger sense of control over the choices they
made and achieved higher automation success rates compared to
both the fully automated baseline agent and OpenAI Operator.
sources.cited_for: Pausing for user decisions can improve control during automated tasks.
sources.not_established: The web-task evaluation does not establish dependable control and recovery across applications and access needs.

shown: Researchers have demonstrated parts of the capability: Apple restored access to some inaccessible mobile apps, Savant simplified desktop commands, and Morae preserved choices during web tasks. These demonstrations remain limited in scope.

OLLA brought accessible agent interaction into everyday desktop use by blind participants. Its results also exposed failures in finding controls, planning actions, and retaining instructions. Broad, faithful access remains a research goal.
missing: Evaluations still need to establish dependable access across unfamiliar software for people with varied sensory and motor needs.
Systems still need to demonstrate that users can follow changes, recover from errors, and reliably resume control across applications.
Tests still need to distinguish faithful interpretation from successful guesses and establish when missing information must be disclosed.

milestones.label: Users complete unfamiliar workflows through their preferred access methods
milestones.explanation: Participants with varied access needs would complete consequential tasks in independently chosen, unseen applications, including software needing adaptation. This would establish breadth within a defined scope.

milestones.label: Task measurements capture understanding and control
milestones.explanation: Evaluations would report access settings, success, effort, time, and errors alongside users’ understanding and ability to regain control. This would reveal whether completion amounts to usable access.

milestones.label: Meaning and user control survive, with information gaps disclosed
milestones.explanation: Tests would demonstrate preserved meaning, clear state changes, user correction and undo where supported, and disclosure of missing information. This would distinguish faithful access from plausible guesses.

milestones.label: Independent evaluations reproduce results and define practical limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would repeat documented tests, broaden coverage, and use justified acceptance criteria set beforehand. This would establish reliability and limits involving native support, user input, access, and privacy.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether any system already delivers the full capability across a clearly defined range of software and access needs.
The application coverage, participant representation, and reliability thresholds needed for a decisive demonstration remain unsettled.
How much task-relevant meaning can be recovered when software exposes too little information remains an open question.
